subject: Business Models
title: Open Source with Enterprise Licensing
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Open Source with Enterprise Licensing.

hook.text: Red Hat gives away its Linux code for free. Then it charges Fortune 500 companies for support.

buildup.text: The open-source core attracts users. Enterprise features—security, support, compliance—cost extra.

discovery.text: IBM bought Red Hat for $34 billion. A company built on free software was worth more than most tech firms.

twist.text: MongoDB and others changed licenses after Amazon sold their open-source software as a paid service.

climax.text: Open source plus enterprise licensing creates powerful funnels: millions try free, thousands pay.

punchline.text: Give away the code. Sell the support. $34 billion model.

quiz.question: How did IBM value Red Hat's free-software business model?

details.summary: Open-source with enterprise licensing gives away core software freely while selling commercial features, support, and managed services to businesses. Red Hat, MongoDB, and Elastic all built billion-dollar businesses by open-sourcing their core product and monetizing enterprise needs.
details.whyItMatters: This model combines open-source adoption speed with enterprise revenue. Free software attracts millions of developers and companies..
takeaways: Core software is free and open-source to maximize adoption
Enterprise features, support, and managed services generate revenue
Developer community adoption drives organic enterprise demand

faq.question: How do open-source companies convert free users to paying enterprise customers?
faq.answer: Enterprise features like SSO, audit logging, advanced security, compliance certifications, and SLA-backed support are available only in paid tiers. As companies scale their use of the open-source product, they need these capabilities and convert to commercial licenses.

faq.question: What challenges do open-source business models face?
faq.answer: Cloud providers can host the open-source software as a managed service without paying the creator, as AWS did with Elasticsearch. Competitors can fork the code. Converting free users to paid is difficult. Some companies have changed licenses to protect against cloud provider exploitation.
